messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings, Avoid Crowds: Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Callum is a 21-year-old single man of European descent who works as a bus driver in a mid-sized American city. He was referred for psychological assessment following a brief conversation with his GP, who had grown concerned after Callum mentioned, almost in passing, that he had not been sleeping well since returning from a military deployment eight months ago. His PCL-5 score of 53 places him firmly in the severe range, and the picture that has emerged across the first few sessions is one of a young man quietly drowning in an experience he cannot yet fully name.

Callum enlisted at eighteen, drawn by a sense of purpose and a family tradition of service. He was deployed as part of a small infantry unit, and it was during a patrol through a village that his world fractured. The unit came under fire, and in the chaos that followed, a vehicle ahead of his was struck by an improvised explosive device. The blast was enormous — a wall of pressure and heat that threw him sideways — and what followed was a scene of burning metal, thick black smoke, and the screaming of men he had trained alongside for months. The smell of burning material and flesh saturated everything. Helicopters arrived to extract the casualties, their rotors cutting through the smoke-filled air. Callum survived physically intact, but something in how he processed that afternoon did not hold together. He has described the event in fragments across sessions — a flash of orange, the particular pitch of a man's voice, the texture of the ground beneath his hands — but the pieces do not cohere into a continuous account. He knows what happened in the way one knows a fact, but when he tries to speak it, the words dissolve. He has sat in silence for long minutes, hands pressed flat on his thighs, unable to continue.

Since returning home, the memories have not receded so much as reorganised themselves into a loop he cannot switch off. They arrive unbidden — a film, as he put it, that plays whether or not he has chosen to watch it. Driving his bus route through the city, Callum has found that the job he took partly for its straightforwardness has become its own minefield. A truck backfiring in traffic can stop him cold, his hands tightening on the wheel as his body responds to a threat that is not there. On two occasions, the sound of a news helicopter passing low over the route has made him pull the bus to the kerb and sit, breathing, until the sound faded. The smell of something burning — a passenger's takeaway bag, a mechanical fault in another vehicle — arrives in his cab without warning and takes him somewhere else entirely.

He has come to believe, with a quiet but immovable certainty, that the world is genuinely dangerous and that his survival depends on remaining alert to that danger at all times. He scans his mirrors constantly, watches passengers with a vigilance that exhausts him by the end of a shift, and has stopped attending the church his family has gone to for three generations, unable to tolerate the enclosed crowd, the incense, or the unpredictability of the congregation around him. He avoids shopping centres entirely and has not attended a single social event since his discharge. In the evenings, he retreats into his phone — hours of games, scrolling, streaming — not because it brings him pleasure, which he notes it no longer does, but because it holds his mind just occupied enough to keep the film from starting. His mother has commented on how much he has withdrawn from the family. He has not been able to explain it to her, partly because he cannot find the words, and partly because he has begun to wonder, in his darker moments, whether any of it is worth explaining at all.

What finally brought Callum to seek help was a near-miss on his route: distracted by the sound of a distant explosion at a construction site, he braked hard and unnecessarily, frightening his passengers. He was written up by his supervisor. Losing this job — the one structure still holding his days together — felt like a line he could not afford to cross. He arrived at his first session guarded and precise, saying only that he needed to get his head right. What he has not yet said aloud, but what sits just beneath the surface of every session, is that he is terrified he no longer knows how.
